en: The Meaning of the Six Identities, composed by the Tiantai monk Xingman in the capital. Regarding the term "identity" (ji):
it signifies that name and essence are non-dual. Now, following the Tiantai Master’s classification of the scriptures into five flavors and four teachings:
Regarding the explanation of these meanings: the three preceding teachings produced from the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) have no such established names.

If that is so, the Hīnayāna of the Tripitaka Teaching analyzes matter to clarify emptiness, which is clearly not the subject under discussion here. As for the Mahāyāna of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), it is the gateway of the Mahāyāna; and as for the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), it is the knowledge of the Middle Way—why, then, are they not explained? Answer:

Because there are differences between the skillful and the clumsy regarding the realms within and beyond [the mundane], the skillful deliverance of the Shared Teaching clarifies emptiness through form (*rūpa*).

If one has merely severed the afflictions of the four abodes within the realm of desire but has not yet shattered delusion, one cannot yet achieve the perfect fusion of the three truths or possess all Buddha-dharmas;

nor can it be said that the initial thought-moment of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is able to perfectly contemplate the three truths, wherein object and wisdom are darkly unified—three in one and one in three—and thus, because cause and effect are fully present, it may be termed "immediate" (ji). If this is so...

Question: If cause and effect are of one essence, how can there be six? Answer: That which is called "identical" (*ji*) is said to distinguish [the essence] from what is separate; that which is called "six" is said to distinguish [the categories] from what is confused.
If the distinction between crimson and purple is made clear, then the stages of cultivation and realization will be known (and so forth). Regarding the first, "identity with principle" (*li-ji*):
"principle" refers to the nature of reality, which is the Tathāgatagarbha inherently possessed from the beginning and not merely acquired now; it is also called "Buddha."

The nature of nature (*xing-xing*) has the meaning of cause, while the Buddha has the meaning of fruit. Because the nature of a person as fruit is already fully present within the cause, it is called "Buddha-nature" and designated as "the Buddha in the sense of principle" (*li-ji*).
As the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature," states:

"It is like a poor man whose house contains a treasury of pure gold, yet none of his family members, great or small, know of its existence. This is the meaning of that passage. Second is "the Buddha in name only" (*ming-zi-ji*).
Whether through a scripture or through a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one hears this name and develops deep faith in this principle, thereby acceding to the Dharma of the Three Truths;

such a person is called a "first person of sympathetic joy" (*prathama-anumodaka*). As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "At that time, there was a different person who well understood skillful means (*upāya*).

This refers precisely to that meaning. Regarding those who practice the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), from the very beginning of sympathetic joy, they deeply contemplate the Three Truths; thus, their words and deeds are in accord with one another.

In accordance with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is called the stage of the Five Grades of Disciples (*pañca-vidha-śrāvaka*), wherein the practices for self-cultivation and the transformation of others are fully perfected in both principle and fact.
As the Sūtra says: "I now employ you; you may weed out the weeds and filth for me"—this is precisely its meaning. Fourth is the stage of semblance realization (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*):

from the stage of contemplative practice (*ālocana-karma-bhūmi*), one enters the path of semblance. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls this the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), by which one is able to [perceive] the wondrous...
The *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* states: "If you can show me my son’s treasury of true gold, only then shall I quickly act for you.

This is precisely that meaning. Furthermore, the "fivefold true realization" (*pañca-vidha-bhūta-prativedha*) is also called the stage of partial realization and similarity (*pratilambha-niṣyanda-avasthā*).
Entering the Dharma of the Copper Wheel is termed "opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision," which refers to the first stage and the first chapter.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) can accomplish the Path through eight aspects; arising from the Truth (*tathatā*), it manifests as the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to teach and transform sentient beings across hundreds of Buddha-worlds.
This is precisely the meaning of what the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "This person immediately digs up a treasury of gold within his own home, and when the woman sees it, her heart gives rise to joy.
Sixth is the "Ultimate" (*niṣṭhāgata*) stage: the forty-two positions reach ultimate perfection, from the first letter *A* to the last...
The syllable *ḍa* has no words by which it can be explained; it is the perfection of wisdom and severance, like the moonlight on the fifteenth day when the moon is full.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Wandering through the four quarters, one proceeds directly to the place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:

"One conceives of such a person with a sense of wonder and marvels at them, looking up to them as the Tathāgata of Wondrous Enlightenment dwelling in the Light of Eternal Quiescence. This is precisely that meaning.

Based on the Master Zhizhe’s (Zhang’an) commentary, which interprets the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* according to the meaning and intent of the Great Master [Zhiyi], this single passage is cited as containing all six stages complete.
What need is there for further extensive explanations scattered throughout various texts?

The lineage of our school must understand that the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the ultimate truth by opening up the six levels of "immediate" realization (*liu ji*), while the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s "clarified butter" (*tihu*) naturally returns one to the secret treasury. If one now clings to the real, one will be deluded regarding the provisional.

With hands folded upright and unmoving, the path is already so long that reaching the treasure-store is difficult to expect; I have briefly outlined the grand principles, and for a detailed clarification, one must consult a separate record.
(End of the Section on the Six Stages of Realization)
